A Type Ia supernova can shine like 5 billion Suns. 💥

A white dwarf pulls gas from a companion until it nears 1.4 times the Sun's mass, carbon ignites and the whole star is blown apart. At its peak it outshines a small galaxy, about three times the Large Magellanic Cloud, while the shock wave races out at around 10,000 km/s. It flings iron, silicon and calcium into space, and over millions of years that gas forms new stars and planets. You carry about 1 kg of calcium, and most of it was forged in exploding stars.

Your skeleton is built from the ash of dead stars.

Your 4 grams of iron was forged in exploding stars. ⭐

After the Big Bang there was almost only hydrogen and helium. Stars fused carbon and oxygen, but most iron comes from exploding stars, where nickel-56 decays into iron over months. That iron drifted for billions of years, then ended up in the cloud that became the Sun and Earth, and finally in your blood.

About 43,000 billion billion iron atoms, every one older than the Sun. About 90 percent of your mass was made in stars.

A rainbow is really a full circle. 🌈

Sunlight enters a raindrop, reflects once inside and leaves about 138° from where it came in. That puts every colour 42° from the point opposite the sun, so the drops at that angle trace a ring of 42° radius. The horizon cuts it; from a plane nothing does, and you see the whole circle around the shadow of your plane. Red sits outside, violet inside, about 1.8° apart.

That ring around the Sun is always 22° out, and ice crystals are the reason. 🌈

Never look straight at the Sun: hide it behind your hand and look about two fists out.

If you dried up the oceans, their salt could bury the continents roughly 150 metres deep. 🌊

Every year about 500,000 km³ of water evaporates from Earth: 41 Lake Superiors. 🌊

At any moment the whole sky holds only about 12,900 km³ of vapour (one lake), so its water is replaced about every 9 days. Ten scent molecules, one wall removed, and nothing pushes them. So why does the smell spread? 🧪

Each molecule is left or right: 2^10 = 1,024 arrangements, and only 1 has all ten back on the left (about 0.1 %), while 252 have five and five. caption:
An ant at 1 cm/s can finish a band whose end races away at 1 km/s. 🐜

The band starts 1 km long and its far end moves 1 km/s, 100,000 times faster than the ant. But stretching carries the ant along, so it never loses its share of the band: it covers 1/100,000 of it each second at 1 km, 1/200,000 at 2 km, 1/300,000 at 3 km. These shares add up like 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ..., which never stops growing (ten terms make 2.93, a thousand make 7.49). By the age of the universe (4.4×10^17 s, 13.8 billion years) the ant has covered only 0.04%, yet it arrives after about 10^43,429 seconds.

caption:
A 7.2° shadow measured the whole Earth. 🌍

In 240 BC, at noon in Syene, the Sun stood straight overhead: no shadow, sunlight on the bottom of a well. At the same noon in Alexandria, a vertical stick cast a shadow and the Sun's ray leaned 7.2° from it. Sun rays arrive parallel, so that same angle opens at Earth's centre, and 7.2° out of 360° is one fiftieth. The cities are 5,000 stadia apart, so the circumference is 50 × 5,000 = 250,000 stadia. Taking a stadion as roughly 157.5 m (uncertain), that is 39,375 km, within two percent of the true 40,008 km pole to pole.

The angles and numbers are computed from the figures above; the stadion length is an assumed value, and the sticks are not to scale.

caption:
A 55.1 µs flicker timed the speed of light. ⚡

In 1849, Fizeau shone a beam through one gap of a 720-tooth wheel at a mirror 8.6 km away. Spin the wheel slowly and the returning light slips through the same gap. At 12.6 turns per second a tooth blocks it and the light goes dark, so the round trip took exactly the time a gap needs to become a tooth: 1 / (2 × 720 × 12.6) = 55.1 µs. Light covered 17.27 km in that time, so its speed is 17.27 km / 55.1 µs = 313,000 km/s, about 4.5 % above the modern 299,792 km/s.

The wheel-face strip is shown 25,000× slower, and the 8,633 m path is not drawn to scale.

caption:
A top spinning at 100 rev/s stays up. Gravity is not the end of the story. 🌀

Gravity acts at the centre of mass, 4 cm from the tip, so it exerts a torque τ = mgr sin θ = 0.0225 N m (m = 0.10 kg, tilt θ = 35°). That torque points sideways, at right angles to the angular momentum L = Iω = 0.0196 kg m²/s, so it turns L instead of shortening it: the axis sweeps a cone at Ω = mgr/Iω = 2.00 rad/s, one lap every 3.14 s (fast-spin approximation). Below about 24 rev/s at this tilt there is no steady precession, and at 10 rev/s the top topples (shown in slow motion). Faster spin, slower precession.

caption:
A pull of about 150 nanonewtons weighed the entire Earth. 🌍

In London in 1798, Cavendish hung a six-foot rod on a thin wire, a lead ball of 0.73 kg at each end, and parked a 158 kg lead ball beside each. Their pull is about 1/47,000,000 of a small ball's own weight, so the wire barely twists; he watched through a telescope from another room so body heat could not stir the air. The twist gives the force, Newton's law then gives G (about 6.7 × 10⁻¹¹), and g = GM/R² gives Earth's mass: about 6 × 10²⁴ kg, 5.5 times as dense as water.
